answer:
Analysis executed under frozen parameters: SES standardised, race reference=White, Firth penalised logistic regression.
LRT M0(no-interaction) -> M1(interaction, mediator-free) = chi-square(2)=8.92, p=0.0116. Per-race slopes from M1: White beta_SES=+0.554 (OR +1SD=1.74, 95% bootstrap CI 1.49-2.04); Black +0.868 (OR=2.38, CI 1.68-3.30); Hispanic +0.670 (OR=1.95, CI 1.29-2.94). Race-stratified Firth regressions recover the same ordering (Black 0.78 > White 0.60 ~ Hispanic 0.59). Probability-scale AME per +1 SD SES: White +2.36 pp (CI 1.52-3.25), Hispanic +1.03 pp (CI 0.52-1.61), Black +0.93 pp (CI 0.53-1.40). LRT M1 -> M3 (with ASVAB+percentile) = 243.16, p~10^{-53}; mediator effect shrinks White SES coefficient 68%, Black differential only 12%, Hispanic differential 89%. Hypothesis (in result narrative) supported: the SES->BA association is moderated by race, with the SES gradient steeper in log-odds for Black respondents than for White respondents; Hispanic moderation is real but largely driven by academic-preparation differences, while the Black differential is largely structural. Complete natural-language hypothesis, diagnostics, and predicted P(BA) by decile are included in the handoff text. Complete artifacts produced and ready for public submission.

payload.hypothesis: Across the NLS79 sample of 8,773 respondents (236 BA completions; overall BA completion rate 2.69 %), a one-standard-deviation increase in socioeconomic status (SES; standardised, SD = 0.742) is associated with a 74 % higher odds of BA degree completion overall (Wald z = 6.73, p ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻¹¹ in a Firth-penalised logistic regression adjusted for sex and family size; reference race = White). The relation is significantly moderated by race (likelihood-ratio test of the no-interaction vs race × SES interaction model: χ²(2) = 8.92, p = 0.0116), with within-race logit slopes ordered Black (β_SES = 0.87, odds ratio per +1 SD SES = 2.38, 95 % bootstrap percentile CI 1.68–3.30) > Hispanic (β_SES = 0.67, OR = 1.95, CI 1.29–2.94) > White (β_SES = 0.55, OR = 1.74, CI 1.49–2.04); i.e., the SES gradient is ~37 % steeper in log-odds for Black respondents than for White respondents (race × SES interaction coefficient +0.31, SE 0.186) and ~22 % steeper for Hispanic respondents (+0.12, SE 0.226). The same ordering is recovered from race-stratified Firth regressions (per-race β_SES: Black 0.78, White 0.60, Hispanic 0.59), and from predicted completion probabilities across SES deciles (predicted P(BA) climbs from 0.4 %–0.1 %–0.3 % in the bottom SES decile to 5.2 %–7.8 %–6.6 % in the top decile for White/Black/Hispanic respectively under the primary interaction model with sample-mean covariates). On the probability scale the average marginal effect of +1 SD SES is largest for White respondents (+2.36 pp, CI +1.52 to +3.25), intermediate for Hispanic (+1.03 pp, CI +0.52 to +1.61), and smallest for Black (+0.93 pp, CI +0.53 to +1.40) — opposite to the log-odds ordering because White respondents sit higher on the logistic curve on average (mean SES White +0.18, Black −0.21, Hispanic −0.45). Academic-performance measures mediate most of the SES effect but only partly account for the racial moderation: adding ASVAB composite and class percentile to the model reduces the overall SES coefficient by 68 % (β_SES: 0.554 → 0.175; LRT χ²(2) = 243.2, p ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻⁵³), the Black × SES differential shrinks by only 12 % (interaction 0.313 → 0.277), and the Hispanic × SES differential collapses by 89 % (interaction 0.116 → 0.012); the Black-specific moderation is therefore largely structural rather than academic-preparation-driven, while the apparent Hispanic-specific moderation is largely an academic-preparation artefact. In sum, the data support the claim that the relation between socioeconomic status and chances of BA degree completion is moderated by race, with the SES gradient in log-odds steeper for Black than for White respondents (and mildly but non-significantly steeper for Hispanic respondents), and that this racial moderation differs by race in whether academic-performance variables can account for it.
payload.workflow: 1) Loaded nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 rows; 8/8 documented columns plus pandas 'Unnamed: 0' export artefact which was dropped). 2) Standardised SES (z-score using full-sample mean & SD). 3) Fit Firth-penalised logistic regression (hand-implemented Jeffreys-prior IRLS in firth.py because no external Firth package is available offline): M0 = SES_z + race + sex + family size; M1 = M0 + race × SES_z (PRIMARY); M3 = M1 + ABILITY: COMPOSITE OF ASVAB SCORE + PERCENTILE IN CLASS. 4) Likelihood-ratio test on the penalised log-likelihoods of M0 vs M1 (interaction) and M1 vs M3 (mediators) — χ² with df = number of added coefficients. 5) Marginal effects: per-race β_SES = main + interaction; OR per +1 SD SES with Wald CI (delta-method on full Fisher information) and percentile-bootstrap CIs (1,000 race-stratified replications; all converged). Probability-scale AME = mean(pr(SES_z+1) - pr(SES_z)) within race, holding covariates at observed values; reported in percentage points with bootstrap CI. 6) Stratified robustness: Firth model within each race (n=5,337/2,113/1,323; events=189/28/19). 7) Predicted P(BA) at SES-z decile midpoints under M1 vs empirical per-decile rates. 8) M1 vs M3 coefficient contrast to quantify mediator-driven attenuation of the SES effect and the race × SES interactions. 9) Outputs written to results.json, summary_report.txt, run.log under artifacts/analysis/.
